sources.news_title: US accuses government contractor of leaking classified info to girlfriend's Substack
TOP-SECRET Leak Case: FBI Nabs CIA Contractor Accused of Passing Intelligence to ‘Journalist’ Girlfriend Behind Substack Posts – 100PercentFedUp.com – by Isaac
sources.text:
The FBI has arrested a CIA contractor accused of reaching into classified intelligence systems, pulling TOP-SECRET reports that had nothing to do with his job and feeding the information to his journalist girlfriend for publication on Substack.
Ian A. Brinksman, 42, was taken into custody after agents searched his Washington, D.C., home.
He now faces a federal charge of unlawfully transmitting national-defense information.
According to prosecutors, this was not one careless conversation. The criminal complaint describes a months-long pattern involving five intelligence reports, repeated phone contact and online stories that allegedly carried classified information from those reports.
The Justice Department announced the arrest and made clear why it views the alleged conduct as a direct threat to American security:
🚨 U.S. Government Contractor Arrested for Allegedly Leaking National Defense Information
“National defense information is classified to protect the American people from bad actors around the world who wish to do us harm,” said @AGToddBlanche. “The details alleged in this… pic.twitter.com/86BfOmQUkx
— U.S. Department of Justice (@TheJusticeDept) October 23, 2026
The Justice Department says Brinksman worked for a federal agency beginning in 2020 before becoming a systems-integration developer for a contractor supporting that same agency in 2022. CIA Director John Ratcliffe identified the agency as the CIA and said it referred the alleged unauthorized disclosures to the FBI.
Brinksman held a Top Secret clearance with Sensitive Compartmented Information access. Prosecutors allege that he used that access to obtain some of the country’s most tightly guarded material and passed it to a romantic partner who intended to publish it.
The partner is identified in the official complaint only as “Individual 1,” a writer who operates an independent publication on Substack. The filing says her own fundraising pitch claimed that she had published reporting based on classified CIA assessments.
The bureau’s warning was blunt: protecting American secrets remains a top counterintelligence priority.
Earlier today, the @FBI arrested a government contractor after he was caught allegedly betraying his oath and leaking classified defense information on at least one occasion.
Protecting America’s secrets is a top counterintelligence priority of this FBI. Anyone caught abusing…
— FBI Director Kash Patel (@FBIDirectorKash) October 24, 2026
The FBI affidavit traces five alleged leak sequences using classified-database records, phone logs, badge swipes, emails and publication dates. It says Brinksman worked inside a secure facility where personal phones were prohibited and his ordinary duties involved moving data between classified and unclassified systems.
Investigators say Individual 1 called Brinksman on March 11. Less than an hour later, he accessed a TOP-SECRET report twice.
A Substack article published that day allegedly contained classified information reflecting the same report. An original classification authority reviewed the article and confirmed the alleged overlap, according to the filing.
The complaint describes similar sequences in May, July and October: phone calls, access to reports marked TOP SECRET, short trips outside the secure facility, more calls and then publication of articles with overlapping information.
Investigators say the brief exits gave Brinksman enough time to reach a personal phone kept outside the secure workspace. The complaint does not rely on timing alone; it also cites the content overlap between the reports and the published articles.
None of the five reports was within the scope of Brinksman’s work, according to the agency. All five carried TS/SCI markings—the classification reserved for material whose unauthorized disclosure could cause exceptionally grave damage to national security.
Phone records cited by the FBI show more than 800 calls or attempted calls between Brinksman and Individual 1 during 2026.
Agency records also showed that Brinksman was among no more than six people who accessed the Substack publication from the federal facility during the period under review. Investigators say he was the only one who both viewed all five articles and accessed all five underlying reports.
The FBI’s own public alert put the arrest and the alleged publication chain on the record:
#NewsAlert: U.S. Government Contractor Arrested for Allegedly Leaking National Defense Information
A U.S. government contractor was arrested by the FBI this morning for allegedly leaking national defense information to another individual who repeatedly posted classified… pic.twitter.com/cj5wkMupTP
— FBI (@FBI) October 24, 2026
Then there is the notebook.
Law enforcement reviewed a notebook left on Brinksman’s desk and found that corners had been torn from several pages. The FBI agent wrote that people sometimes take notes so they can later pass along verbatim or near-verbatim information.
The affidavit also cites an earlier email in which Brinksman allegedly told a friend that the journalist he was dating had gone independent and that he had been helping get her foreign-policy venture off the ground.
Investigators documented one separate article the pair allegedly edited together through a shared Google document. The government said it had not identified classified material in that particular article at the time of the filing.
The charged conduct is the alleged willful transmission of national-defense information to someone not entitled to receive it.
Attorney General Todd Blanche said the Justice Department will keep prosecuting people who leak classified information and put national security at risk. Ratcliffe said there is zero tolerance for unauthorized disclosures that endanger intelligence sources, operations and CIA officers.
Brinksman is charged by criminal complaint, and the allegations must still be proven in court. He is presumed innocent unless and until a jury finds otherwise.
But the evidence described by the FBI is not vague. It is a timeline built from classified-database logs, phone records, badge swipes, emails, publication dates and the defendant’s own workplace access.
If prosecutors prove their case, an insider used extraordinary access to funnel America’s secrets into a girlfriend’s publishing operation rather than use lawful whistleblower channels.
The allegation is a national-security betrayal, and the FBI says it finally caught up with the man behind it.
This is a Guest Post from our friends over at WLTReport. View the original article here.

sources.news_title: FBI Arrests CIA Contractor Accused of Leaking TOP-SECRET Intelligence to His ‘Journalist’ Girlfriend — Classified Information Allegedly Published on Substack * The Gateway Pundit * by Jim Hᴏft
sources.text:
The FBI has arrested a CIA contractor accused of systematically pulling TOP SECRET national defense information outside the scope of his duties and feeding it to his romantic partner, a left-leaning independent journalist who published matching material on her Substack newsletter.
Ian A. Brinksman, 42, of Washington, D.C., was taken into custody Friday following a search of his residence and charged by criminal complaint with unlawfully transmitting national defense information in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 793(d). The case was filed in the Eastern District of Virginia, Alexandria Division, Newsmax reported.
An Original Classification Authority has confirmed that five Substack articles contained classified information reflecting the contents of TOP SECRET reports Brinksman accessed, some carrying TS/SCI banners that by definition could cause exceptionally grave damage to national security if disclosed without authorization.
According to the sworn FBI affidavit by Special Agent John W. Althen, Brinksman held a TS/SCI clearance and worked inside a SCIF for a U.S. government agency (identified in public reporting and by CIA Director John Ratcliffe as the CIA) beginning around 2020 before shifting in September 2022 to a systems integration developer role for a third-party contractor supporting the same agency.
His duties included data transfers between classified and unclassified systems. None of the five reports he accessed were within the scope of his work.
The affidavit details a repeating pattern across 2026: contact with “Individual 1” (identified in contemporaneous reporting as Aída Chávez, founder of the Capital & Empire Substack), followed by Brinksman accessing a TOP SECRET report in the classified database, additional calls, and then a Substack post with overlapping content.
Phone records show more than 800 calls or attempted calls between the pair this year. Badge-swipe data, facility entry/exit logs, and short windows outside the secure facility (where personal cell phones are not permitted) align with the communications.
On one occasion, law enforcement noted a notebook left on Brinksman’s desk with corners of several pages torn out, consistent with note-taking for later transmission of near-verbatim material.
Specific sequences include:
- March 11: Call from Individual 1 at 8:41 a.m., Brinksman accesses Report 1 (TOP SECRET) at 9:09 a.m. and 10:01 a.m., facility exits and re-entries, evening call, then Article 1 posted the same day containing classified content.
- May 12: Morning call, access to Report 2, exit, multiple afternoon calls, Article 2 the next day.
- May 26, July 28, August access to Report 5, and October 1: similar access-call-publication chains culminating in Article 5 around October 5.
Chávez has described her Substack as reporting on “Congress, War, and political economy.” In a September 2026 fundraising piece she wrote that over the past year she had “published reporting based on classified CIA assessments that I believe the public deserves to know about.”
Her social media profile included the statement “I also accept leaks.” A November 2025 email from Brinksman’s Gmail to a friend stated he was “helping her get that off the ground” after she “recently went independent,” noting her focus on foreign policy and the “enrichment/fulfilment” he was getting from the work.
Emails and other records establish the personal relationship. Brinksman also co-edited at least one separate article with her via Google Docs on Middle East geopolitics (no classified equities identified in that piece).
As a clearance holder he was required to seek prepublication review; investigators found he had done so for co-authored pieces.
Chávez previously worked as The Nation’s D.C. correspondent and covered Congress for The Intercept. Her publication’s about page describes reporting through a “Marxist and anti-imperialist lens.” She has not been charged. A federal public defender representing Brinksman declined comment.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe stated the investigation followed a referral from the agency: “The unauthorized release of classified material poses grave risks to our national security, intelligence sources, ongoing operations, and our officers.” Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg said Brinksman “reached far outside his own duties to obtain some of our Nation’s most closely held secrets and handed them to a romantic partner he knew intended to publish them. That is not carelessness. It is a betrayal of his oath and the American people who entrusted him to fulfill his duties honorably.”
Attorney General Todd Blanche added that the Department of Justice will continue prosecuting individuals who leak classified information and put national security at risk. FBI Director Kash Patel emphasized that protecting America’s secrets is a top counterintelligence priority and that anyone abusing a position of trust will face the full weight of justice.

sources.news_title: CIA Contractor Arrested After Allegedly Leaking Nation’s ‘Most Closely Held Secrets’ To Romantic Partner
sources.text:
A U.S. government contractor was arrested Friday morning after he allegedly leaked classified information to a romantic partner.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) arrested District of Columbia resident Ian Brinksman, 42, for allegedly leaking national defense information to a woman he knew intended to publish classified information through her online Substack newsletter, the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) stated in a Friday press release. (RELATED: Pentagon Reportedly Escalates Hunt For Leakers By Ordering Polygraph Exams)
The DOJ did not immediately respond to the Daily Caller News Foundation’s request for comment.
🚨 U.S. Government Contractor Arrested for Allegedly Leaking National Defense Information “National defense information is classified to protect the American people from bad actors around the world who wish to do us harm,” said @AGToddBlanche. “The details alleged in this affidavit reflect the behavior of a government contractor who exempted himself from a federal law governing the protection of classified information. The Department of Justice will continue prosecuting individuals who leak classified information and put our national security at risk.” Read more: https://t.co/uTDo8tiSjA
— U.S. Department of Justice (@TheJusticeDept) October 23, 2026
“The FBI arrested the subject after he was caught allegedly betraying his oath and leaking classified defense information,” FBI Director Kash Patel states in the release. “Protecting America’s secrets is a top counterintelligence priority of this FBI - and anyone caught abusing their position of trust within the government by jeopardizing national security and putting our brave warriors at risk will be met with the full weight of justice.”
Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) Director John Ratcliffe also stated that the defendant provided services to the CIA as a contractor.
“The unauthorized release of classified material poses grave risks to our national security, intelligence sources, ongoing operations, and our officers,” Ratcliffe notes. “There is absolutely zero tolerance for leaking, and anyone who violates their oath will be held accountable and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”
Brinksman worked for a U.S. government agency based in the Eastern District of Virginia beginning in 2020 before he started working as a government contractor for that same agency in 2022 as a developer for systems integration with a Top Secret security clearance, according to the criminal complaint.
At the time of writing, what appears to be Brinksman’s LinkedIn profile claimed he worked for the U.S. Department of State as a foreign service officer beginning in February 2020 before working for Deloitte as a senior strategy consultant in August 2022. It also claimed he has been an intelligence officer for the U.S. Navy since March 2020.
Brinksman, in November 2025, began dating a woman investigators believe is a journalist who started a Substack account focused on “Congress, War, and political economy.” Notably, she posted “I also accept leaks,” according to the affidavit. He allegedly contributed to five of her articles from March 11 through Oct. 5 containing Top Secret other highly classified information.
Brinksman, who authorities charged under the Espionage Act, could face up to ten years in prison if convicted.
Editor’s note: This report’s headline was updated.

sources.news_title: Top-secret CIA contractor accused of handing girlfriend 'most closely held secrets'
sources.text:
A government contractor with top-secret access is facing federal charges after allegedly feeding classified intelligence to someone he was dating.
The FBI arrested Ian Brinksman, a Washington resident who did contract work for the CIA, on Friday after searching his home, the Justice Department announced. Prosecutors allege he passed national defense information to a romantic partner who runs a newsletter on Substack.
"As alleged, Brinksman reached far outside his own duties to obtain some of our Nation's most closely held secrets and handed them to a romantic partner he knew intended to publish them," Assistant Attorney General John Eisenberg, who leads the department's National Security Division, said in a statement. "That is not carelessness. It is a betrayal of his oath."
Brinksman went to work for an unnamed U.S. government agency in 2020 and moved in 2022 to a job as a systems integration developer at a private contractor serving that same agency, according to the complaint. Throughout that time, he held a Top Secret clearance with access to Sensitive Compartmented Information.
An FBI agent's sworn affidavit says he repeatedly pulled up classified intelligence reports and then made contact with his partner, identified only as "Individual 1." Investigators point to phone records, badge-swipe data, database logs and emails, and they allege that on at least five occasions this year she published articles mirroring the classified reports, some marked top secret.
Washington Examiner reporter Kaelan Deese, citing the affidavit, reported via X that investigators tracked more than 800 calls or attempted calls between the pair in 2026. Deese also noted that a LinkedIn profile under Brinksman's name lists stints at Deloitte and a current post as a U.S. Navy reserve intelligence officer.
The affidavit quotes a September fundraising post in which Individual 1 claimed to have "published reporting based on classified" agency assessments. According to the Justice Department, she also wrote on social media, "I also accept leaks."
Reuters reported that the quoted language matches a Sept. 28 post on Capital & Empire, a newsletter written by former Nation journalist Aída Chávez, and Deese said a source told him the newsletter was a match. Chávez did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment, and a federal public defender representing Brinksman declined to comment.
Capital & Empire has published multiple stories describing classified CIA assessments, including an Oct. 5 report, co-published with Drop Site News, describing a CIA analysis that warned Israel could slide into civil conflict. The Justice Department has not said which articles are tied to the case.

sources.text:
A classified U.S. intelligence assessment warning that Israel could descend into civil conflict, claims that Israeli officials pressed the Trump administration to assassinate a senior Iranian leader, and a secret report detailing efforts to secure American military support beyond Donald Trump's presidency are among the revelations at the center of a major intelligence leak scandal in Washington. 
On Friday, the FBI arrested a CIA contractor suspected of passing classified information to his journalist girlfriend, whose reporting included five stories based on sensitive intelligence, three of them directly concerning Israel.
The suspect, Ian A. Brinksman, 42, of Washington, D.C., held a Top Secret security clearance with access to highly sensitive intelligence. Prosecutors allege that for months he exploited his access to U.S. intelligence systems to examine classified reports unrelated to his duties and pass information to his romantic partner, who operated an independent news publication on Substack. Investigators linked his access to sensitive documents with telephone conversations between the couple and the publication dates of articles allegedly containing information from those reports.
American authorities have not publicly identified the journalist, referred to in the FBI affidavit as "Individual 1," or disclosed the subjects of the classified reports. However, documents obtained by ynet indicate that she is American journalist Aída Chávez, founder of the independent investigative publication Capital & Empire. Chávez previously worked for The Hill, contributed to The Washington Post and served as a congressional correspondent for The Intercept and Washington correspondent for The Nation. Five articles published on her website match the dates identified in the FBI affidavit, while a passage from a September fundraising appeal appears almost word for word in the document. Chávez has not been charged with any offense in connection with the investigation.
Israel's alleged assassination request and fears of civil war
One of the most significant articles appeared on May 28, under the headline "EXCLUSIVE: Israel Privately Pressing U.S. to Kill Iran's Lead Negotiator and Launch New Strikes." Chávez reported that Israeli officials had urged the Trump administration to assassinate Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the speaker of Iran's parliament and a central figure in negotiations between Tehran and Washington. According to the report, Israel sought to persuade the Americans to abandon negotiations and resume attacks on Iran's oil infrastructure, believing further economic damage could trigger widespread protests and potentially bring down the Iranian regime.
Chávez said her reporting drew on a classified intelligence assessment circulated within the U.S. intelligence community and conversations with officials familiar with its contents. The FBI affidavit states that Brinksman accessed a classified report on May 26 and called his girlfriend three times that day. Two days later, she published an article that investigators say contained information from the same report.
Another article, published on July 29, described a U.S. intelligence assessment concerning Israel's efforts to preserve its strategic relationship with Washington as American public support for Israel weakened. According to Chávez, Israeli officials were seeking to embed their country more deeply within the American military, intelligence and defense industries, making it more difficult for future administrations to reduce cooperation. The reported strategy included discussions about a possible permanent U.S. military base in Israel, expanded joint weapons development and stronger ties with influential American technology executives. Investigators said Brinksman accessed a Top Secret document on July 28, spoke with his girlfriend several times that day and that an article containing information from the document appeared the following day.
The third Israel-related article, published on October 5 in cooperation with Drop Site News, concerned a reported CIA assessment titled "Fracture From Within." According to two American sources cited in the article, the assessment was prepared in August by the CIA's Red Cell, a unit tasked with challenging conventional intelligence assumptions and examining alternative scenarios. It warned that Israel's political crisis, disputes over military conscription for ultra-Orthodox Jewish men, economic pressure, social divisions and the psychological consequences of prolonged warfare could combine to produce severe internal conflict or even institutional breakdown ahead of the October 27 election.
The reported assessment raised concerns about armed military veterans returning from combat with psychological trauma, worsening political polarization and mounting resentment over exemptions from military service. It also examined the possibility of foreign technology companies withdrawing from Israel, deteriorating regional relationships and Hamas or Hezbollah exploiting domestic instability. Crucially, the report did not constitute an official U.S. intelligence prediction that civil war would occur. It was an assessment of potential risks and scenarios, as described by the journalist's sources.
The FBI affidavit details another striking sequence of events. Brinksman allegedly accessed a classified document several times in August and again on October 1. Telephone records show that he spoke with his girlfriend for 47 minutes that day, followed by another conversation lasting 37 minutes. Four days later, the article on Israel's potential internal collapse appeared.
The two remaining articles concerned other Middle Eastern developments. On March 11, Chávez reported that Bahrain had brought in forces from Jordan to help suppress protests over its involvement in the war with Iran. On May 13, she reported on a classified CIA assessment describing divisions among Washington's Gulf allies, with the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain favoring continued strikes against Iran while Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Kuwait preferred renewed negotiations. Investigators allege that classified information accessed by Brinksman also appeared in these reports.
More than 800 calls and a trail of classified documents
The evidence that led investigators to Brinksman is detailed in a 13-page FBI affidavit. He began working for a U.S. government agency in 2020 before moving to a contractor serving the same agency. In 2022, he took a position involving computer systems integration, including work transferring data between classified and unclassified systems. CIA Director John Ratcliffe confirmed that Brinksman had provided services to the agency.
His position required him to work inside a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility, or SCIF, a secure area where personal phones and electronic devices are prohibited. Employees must use identification cards to enter and leave, creating records that became central to the investigation. According to the FBI, Brinksman repeatedly accessed classified reports, left the secure area and contacted his girlfriend, sometimes within minutes. Investigators believe these intervals allowed him to retrieve his personal phone, possibly from his vehicle, and communicate sensitive information.
In one example, the journalist called Brinksman at 8:41 a.m. on March 11. Less than half an hour later, he accessed a classified intelligence report at 9:09 a.m. and again at 10:01 a.m. He subsequently left the secure facility and received another call from her that evening, lasting about 14 minutes. An article published that day allegedly contained Top Secret information from the document he had examined.
Investigators found records of more than 800 telephone calls or attempted calls between the couple during 2026. They also examined computers at Brinksman's workplace and discovered that he was among no more than six people who had accessed the journalist's Substack publication from that facility during the period under investigation. According to the affidavit, no other individual combined access to all five classified reports with visits to all five articles that authorities believe contained information from those documents.
A notebook discovered on Brinksman's desk on October 10 also attracted investigators' attention because corners had been torn from several pages. An FBI agent noted that individuals who transmit sensitive information sometimes write notes to reproduce accurate or near-verbatim quotations. However, the affidavit did not establish that the notebook contained leaked secrets or provide direct evidence that its missing pages had been used to transmit information.
‘I'm helping her build her publication’
One of the most personal details in the investigation emerged from an email Brinksman sent to a friend in November 2025. He described his new relationship with a journalist who had recently become independent and explained that he was helping her establish a publication focused on foreign policy. He added that the project had proved surprisingly fulfilling. Other emails examined by investigators supported the conclusion that the two were romantically involved.
According to the affidavit, their collaboration extended beyond conversations about published stories. On March 13, Brinksman received permission to edit a Google Docs document concerning a Middle Eastern country. Minutes later, he suggested a wording change, which his girlfriend marked as resolved. The article published that day matches a Chávez report concerning Democratic Congressman Josh Gottheimer, a prominent supporter of Israel, and congressional votes related to the war with Iran. Investigators did not identify classified information in that particular article. Brinksman had also sought advance publication clearance, as required of security clearance holders, for articles he co-authored with the journalist.
Brinksman's background adds an unusual dimension to the allegations. A graduate of Georgetown University's School of Foreign Service, he co-authored a study published in May 2019 titled "Millennial Considerations on Insider Threat: Are We A Threat Or An Opportunity?" The research examined the risks posed by employees with access to sensitive information and proposed measures to prevent security breaches, including employee training, monitoring potential warning signs and addressing vulnerabilities associated with social media and mobile technology. Seven years later, Brinksman faces allegations involving precisely the kind of insider threat his research sought to help organizations prevent.
Chávez describes Capital & Empire as an independent publication investigating the interests driving American military and economic policy. In a September fundraising appeal, she said she had published reporting based on classified CIA assessments that she believed the public deserved to know about. She also encouraged readers with inside information to provide leaks.

sources.news_title: FBI arrests Ian Brinksman, government contractor accused of leaking classified defense information to lover - THE LOCAL REPORT ARTICLES
sources.text:
The FBI arrested Ian A. Brinksman, a Washington, DC-based government contractor, on Friday for allegedly transmitting classified national defense information to a romantic partner. The partner later published material online, the US Department of Justice said.
Brinksman, 42, was arrested after an FBI search of his residence and charged through a criminal complaint with unlawfully transmitting national defense information.
The charges alleged that he used his position of trust and access to sensitive government systems to obtain and share classified material.

What is Ian Brinksman accused of?
According to the complaint, Brinksman held a Top Secret security clearance with Sensitive Compartmented Information (SCI) access while working for a US government agency and later as a contractor supporting the same agency.
His LinkedIn profile shows that he currently works as a Manager with Deloitte. He has also previously worked at national security consultancy, and as a reserve intelligence officer for the United States Navy.
Investigators allege he provided classified information to an individual who operated an online publication on Substack and had publicly stated that she accepted leaks. The Justice Department did not publicly identify the online publisher.
A DC Examiner journalist, Kaela Deese, claimed after the arrest that the individual could be journalist Aida Chavez, who has previously covered national security issues. However, those claims have not been confirmed by federal authorities.
Brinksman allegedly maintained personal relationship with Substack publisher
The criminal complaint stated that Brinksman began working for a US government agency in 2020 in Virginia. He joined “Company 1” in 2022 as a developer for systems integration work. The company provided services to the same government agency, according to prosecutors.
The complaint detailed that Brinksman maintained a personal relationship with “Individual 1” (Substack publisher). The complaint stated that the publisher later released reporting based on classified assessments from the government agency connected to Brinksman’s work.
A fundraising article published by Individual 1 in September 2026 reportedly stated that the publication had produced reporting based on classified government assessments. Prosecutors also cited a social media post in which “Individual 1” allegedly wrote, “I also accept leaks.”
Officials said the alleged disclosures involved some of the nation’s most sensitive information. “As alleged, Brinksman reached far outside his own duties to obtain some of our Nation’s most closely held secrets and handed them to a romantic partner he knew intended to publish them,” Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg said.
The FBI said protecting classified information remains a major counterintelligence priority.
“Anyone caught abusing their position of trust within the government by jeopardizing national security and putting our brave warriors at risk will be met with the full weight of justice,” FBI Director Kash Patel said in an X post.

CIA, FBI investigate alleged national security breach
CIA Director John Ratcliffe said the contractor had provided services to the agency and was arrested after a referral from the CIA. He said the release of classified information could threaten intelligence sources, ongoing operations and officers.
“The unauthorized release of classified material poses grave risks to our national security, intelligence sources, ongoing operations, and our officers,” Ratcliffe said.
The FBI Chicago Field Office is leading the investigation with assistance from the Washington Field Office.
